title: Examining contributions of child- and classroom-level processes to cross-linguistic relations of literacy-related skills
text_snippet: Examining contributions of child- and classroom-level processes to cross-linguistic relations of literacy-related skills Abstract This study examined whether cross-linguistic relations among early literacy skills in Spanish and English were consistent with child- or classroom-level processes in emergent bilinguals. Participants were 217 children followed from kindergarten to first grade across two states and instructional contexts (English-only and dual-language). In kindergarten, children completed measures of vocabulary, sentence repetition, rapid letter naming, and phonological awareness in both languages; in first grade, they completed measures of decoding, including word reading and nonword reading. Path analyses predicted first-grade reading outcomes from kindergarten language and code-related skills, first using unmanipulated scores and then using group-mean centered scores to separate child- from classroom-level variance. Results showed cross-language associations for code-related skills (particularly phonological awareness and letter naming), whereas oral language measures showed limited cross-linguistic prediction. title: Parafoveal processing in non-phonetic Chinese reading: evidence from children with and without developmental dyslexia
text_snippet: Parafoveal processing in non-phonetic Chinese reading: evidence from children with and without developmental dyslexia Abstract Efficient parafoveal processing is critical for fluent reading, yet its role in Chinese developmental dyslexia (DD) remains underexplored, particularly among those who learn the script without phonetic scaffolds. This study used the boundary paradigm to examine how parafoveal orthographic, phonological, and semantic information contributes to Chinese sentence reading. Ninety-one children from Hong Kong were divided into three groups: 30 with DD (Primary 4–6), 31 chronological-age-matched (CA; Primary 4–6), and 30 reading-level-matched (RL; Primary 2–3) controls. Eye movements were recorded to assess effects on fixation durations and skipping probability. Across groups, identical and orthographic–phonological (O+P) previews reliably reduced fixation times, highlighting an important role of orthographic information in Chinese parafoveal processing. Semantic previews also elicited first-fixation reductions, suggesting rapid but transient parafoveal access to meaning. Phonological-only previews yielded no reliable preview benefit, indicating that an isolated phonological match did not produce a measurable preview benefit in this non-phonetic instructional context. title: Associations and dissociations of reading and spelling in Hungarian primary school children
text_snippet: Associations and dissociations of reading and spelling in Hungarian primary school children Abstract While reading and spelling are closely related, their selective impairments have also been documented with distinct profiles in rapid automatized naming and phonological awareness. The current study examined the association and dissociation of reading and spelling difficulties in Hungarian, a language with complex agglutinative grammatical structure. In a large sample of Hungarian children ( N = 1908) in Grades 1 to 6, we investigated the association between reading and spelling, as well as the prevalence of isolated and combined deficits. A smaller sample ( N = 178) was reinvited to re-assess their literacy skills and their language-based cognitive abilities in rapid automatized naming, phoneme deletion, and a newly developed inflectional/derivational task. We explored how the language-based abilities explained the dissociation between reading and spelling. Further, we formed four subsamples of children to identify their cognitive profiles: poor readers/poor spellers ( N = 42), poor readers/good spellers ( N = 19), good readers/poor spellers (group, N = 26), and typically developing children ( N = 41). title: Longitudinal factorial stability and growth of foundational reading skills in at-risk and non–at-risk kindergarteners
text_snippet: Longitudinal factorial stability and growth of foundational reading skills in at-risk and non–at-risk kindergarteners Abstract This study examined the longitudinal factorial invariance and growth trajectories of a Spanish curriculum-based measurement (CBM) of foundational reading skills in kindergarten within a Response to Intervention (RtI) framework. A total of 196 Spanish-speaking kindergarteners were assessed at three time points (fall, winter, and spring) on five CBM tasks targeting phonological awareness, alphabetic knowledge, print concepts, and vocabulary. Longitudinal confirmatory factor analyses supported the factorial stability of the IPAL-EI across the kindergarten year, revealing a coherent latent construct with a stable internal organization and demonstrating configural, metric, and scalar invariance. Hierarchical linear modeling revealed significant linear growth across the school year for most CBM indicators and for an omnibus composite score, with the exception of phonological awareness and written language knowledge–text. At-risk students showed significantly lower initial performance across most measures; however, growth trajectories were largely parallel across groups, with limited evidence of differential slopes over time. title: Brazilian teachers’ knowledge of dyslexia, language, and literacy instruction
text_snippet: Brazilian teachers’ knowledge of dyslexia, language, and literacy instruction Abstract This exploratory study assessed Brazilian teachers’ knowledge of dyslexia, linguistics, and reading instruction methods as well as socioeconomic predictors of their performance. Teachers (N = 214) completed a sociodemographic questionnaire and three instruments assessing knowledge of dyslexia, phonology, and reading instruction. Participants worked in public schools, were predominantly female (98.59%), with a mean age of 41.8 years ( SD = 7.98), over ten years of teaching experience, and degrees primarily in Pedagogy. Mean accuracy on the dyslexia items was 67.09%, although 78.5% of participants incorrectly associated reading disability with intelligence. Phonological knowledge was limited (40.3%), particularly in phoneme identification. School location and teaching role predicted teachers’ linguistic knowledge, while additional training emerged as the strongest predictor of dyslexia knowledge. In open-ended questions, the whole-word method was most frequently reported, whereas phonics-based instruction was rarely mentioned and often poorly conceptualized. title: Writing as a window on reading: trait-level outcomes of an integrated reading, writing, and knowledge-building intervention for secondary school students with reading difficulties
text_snippet: Writing as a window on reading: trait-level outcomes of an integrated reading, writing, and knowledge-building intervention for secondary school students with reading difficulties Abstract Adolescent students with reading difficulties face compounding challenges in both reading and writing, yet few interventions address both within content-area instruction. This study examined an integrated reading, writing, and knowledge-building intervention using Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD) across four curriculum topics with 12 secondary school students with reading difficulties. A clustered concurrent multiple-baseline single-case design evaluated writing outcomes using an adapted 6+1 Trait® Writing Rubric. Visual analysis showed immediate level changes replicated across three staggered clusters, with complete observed non-overlap between phases for most students and outcomes; the pattern of gains nevertheless varied by trait. Findings extend SRSD research to secondary school students with reading difficulties and are consistent with, though do not test, the proposition that writing can index knowledge built through sustained curricular reading.

title: Tier 2 racial disparities in reading: An illustration of exploring opportunities and outcomes
text_snippet: Tier 2 racial disparities in reading: An illustration of exploring opportunities and outcomes Abstract Important questions exist about the extent to which racial gaps exist in instructional opportunities and achievement outcomes for elementary students in schools implementing multi-tiered systems of support. In the United States, concerns about gaps for Black and White students are of particular concern. Our work illustrates a systematic evaluation of racial differences in instructional opportunities and outcomes of a high impact tutoring program as implemented across 50 high needs schools in a midwestern state. The program provides high impact tutoring to K-3 students with reading difficulties through well-trained community-based tutors. Although this approach is used in schools in more than a dozen states, the extent to which implementation and outcomes are similar for students of different racial backgrounds has not been systematically examined. Using data from the 2022–23 academic year, we compared various indicators of instructional opportunities (e.g., attendance, intervention changes, materials sent home) and outcomes (e.g., spring reading score, program exit, reading growth) for Black or African American and White students matched on grade and fall reading score. title: Effectiveness of a self-regulated strategy development intervention on reading comprehension and written expression in students with specific learning disabilities affecting reading and writing: an experimental study
text_snippet: Effectiveness of a self-regulated strategy development intervention on reading comprehension and written expression in students with specific learning disabilities affecting reading and writing: an experimental study Abstract Teaching reading and writing strategies presents significant challenges for students with Specific Learning Disabilities (SLD). This research project outlines a 28-hour integrated intervention program that focuses on cognitive and metacognitive strategies for improving Reading Comprehension (RC) and Written Expression (WE) in Greek 5th and 6th graders with SLD. The program was implemented by 19 resource room teachers (experimental and comparison groups) utilizing the Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD) instructional approach, with an additional 14 resource-room teachers teaching the control group. The participants were divided into three groups: an Experimental Group comprising 38 students (taught RC + WE), a Comparison Group with 36 students (taught only WE), and a Control Group with 44 students (business as usual). The study followed a pre-midpoint-post-maintenance experimental design. title: The role of orthographic units and positional consistency in L2 Chinese character writing: Insights from online handwriting tasks
text_snippet: The role of orthographic units and positional consistency in L2 Chinese character writing: Insights from online handwriting tasks Abstract This study employed online handwriting tasks to examine two key components of Chinese orthographic knowledge―a repertoire of orthographic units of different grain sizes and the positional consistency of orthographic units―as well as the relationship between character writing and character knowledge. Fifty adult Korean learners of Chinese as a second language (L2) completed two Chinese character copying tasks—one with real characters and one with pseudo-characters—and a character naming task. Analyses of inter-stroke intervals (ISIs) in the real character copying task revealed a significant boundary effect, with longer pauses occurring between orthographic units than within them, indicating L2 learners’ tendency to chunk characters into functional units during writing. Shorter ISIs for phonetically regular characters demonstrated the potential influence of phonetic regularity on handwriting. Notably, participants showed higher accuracy when copying pseudo-characters containing components with high positional consistency after controlling for HSK levels. title: Who responds to surveys assessing teachers’ specialized knowledge to teach literacy?Implications for generalization and representation
text_snippet: Who responds to surveys assessing teachers’ specialized knowledge to teach literacy?Implications for generalization and representation Abstract The growing research base concerning the role of teachers’ specialized knowledge to teach literacy in supporting students’ reading achievement—and policies based on this research—primarily relies on data from teacher knowledge surveys. We examined the possibility that teachers who respond to knowledge surveys are systematically different from teachers who only partially or do not respond. In this exploratory study, we examined response patterns (complete, partially complete, no response) to teacher knowledge surveys in three U.S.-based projects and explored potential differences among response patterns based on sociodemographic characteristics, teaching beliefs, and classroom/program characteristics. We identified response patterns using missing value analyses and applied the What Works Clearinghouse guidelines for group equivalency. Collectively, these projects represent data from ~ 870 inservice and preservice preschool-Grade 5 teachers. Across datasets, 84% of teachers completed the surveys, 10% partially completed, and 7% were nonresponders. title: Bidirectional associations between classroom and support teacher perceptions and reading speed in students with reading difficulties: a longitudinal study
text_snippet: Bidirectional associations between classroom and support teacher perceptions and reading speed in students with reading difficulties: a longitudinal study Abstract Teacher perceptions have been conceptualized as a critical interpersonal mechanism mediating the effects of classroom interactions on student learning. However, several questions remain regarding the differential impact of ability and engagement perceptions, how their association with reading achievement unfolds, and whether they differ between distinct teacher groups, particularly within the context of intervention programs. This study examined how classroom- and support-teacher perceptions were associated with reading speed, the distinctiveness of ability and engagement perceptions, and differences between classroom and support teachers. Two hundred and eighty second-grade students with reading difficulties enrolled in the A to Z intervention program were followed across one school year using longitudinal cross-lagged models. Classroom teachers rated students’ reading ability and engagement, while support teachers rated their engagement. For classroom teachers, the results revealed reciprocal links: reading speed predicted perceptions of reading ability and engagement, and perceptions of ability in turn predicted subsequent reading speed. title: Impact of executive functions on learning to read in the early stages of development
text_snippet: Impact of executive functions on learning to read in the early stages of development Abstract Studies conducted in recent years have confirmed the importance of phonological awareness as one of the most robust predictors of early reading. However, alongside this knowledge, there is no work that has focused on analyzing how to maximize its effects on the literacy process. It is known that certain cognitive skills, particularly executive functions, exert a decisive influence on school learning and, especially, on reading. However, there is no work focused on understanding the combined impact of both skills on early reading. Hence the objective of this study, which aims to analyze the potential that combined instruction in phonological awareness and executive functions can have on early reading learning. A quasi-experimental design was used, comparing groups with pretest and posttest measures. The study included 386 students between the ages of 6 and 8. The results indicate that the joint stimulation of phonological awareness and certain executive functions, such as working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility, promotes improved reading learning. title: A proposal for adapting tiered models of support to foreign language writing instruction
text_snippet: A proposal for adapting tiered models of support to foreign language writing instruction Abstract The Multi-Tiered System of Support (MTSS) is a preventive framework that has demonstrated its effectiveness in early literacy instruction. However, its applicability to foreign language writing teaching has yet to be explored. The present study aims to address this educational shortcoming. A total of 132 students from fourth, fifth, and sixth grades of primary education were asked to write a narrative in English as a foreign language (EFL). The texts were analyzed according to the types of errors produced. This enabled four distinct writing profiles to be identified, corresponding to the tiers of support within the MTSS: Strong Writers (47.73%, Tier 1), Grammar-Weak Writers (32.58%, Tier 2), Spelling-Weak Writers (12.88%, Tier 2), and Poor Writers (6.82%, Tier 3). These findings suggest that the MTSS model can be effectively adapted to narrative writing instruction in EFL contexts. Furthermore, in the absence of standardized assessment tools, analyzing errors in written narratives could provide a practical method for categorizing students into these tiers. title: An analysis of multilingual writing quality: the use of connectives in expository texts in Basque, Spanish, and English
text_snippet: An analysis of multilingual writing quality: the use of connectives in expository texts in Basque, Spanish, and English Abstract This study examines how mid-adolescent students (ages 13–15) use connectives in expository writing across Basque, Spanish, and English, and whether such use predicts writing quality. Expository writing is a key academic genre in secondary education, and understanding how multilingual students deploy linguistic resources such as connectives is essential for characterising their writing development. The dataset included 136 students’ 408 expository texts (one per language per student) and scores from the Academic Language Proficiency (ALP) test, along with SES, gender, L1, and exposure to Basque as control variables. Descriptive, correlational, and regression analyses indicated that a higher frequency of analytic connectives was positively associated with writing quality, although this relationship varied across languages. In particular, analytic connectives emerged as significant predictors in some languages after controlling for sociodemographic factors, ALP, text length, and the use of basic connectives, whereas in English writing quality was primarily predicted by ALP. title: Modeling longitudinal growth in handwriting fluency: the role of pencil grip, writing task, and risk status in early education
text_snippet: Modeling longitudinal growth in handwriting fluency: the role of pencil grip, writing task, and risk status in early education Abstract This longitudinal study examined how pencil grip maturity and task demands jointly shape the development of handwriting fluency, defined as the integration of speed and accuracy, in a sample of 290 Spanish-speaking children assessed from early childhood education through the end of second grade. Across five measurement points, children completed two handwriting tasks: letter copying and name writing. Twelve grip types were identified and classified into three developmental levels: primitive, transitional, and mature. Generalized additive mixed models showed that children using mature grips consistently exhibited higher fluency and steeper growth trajectories than those with transitional or primitive grips did, particularly in the name-writing task. These differences became most pronounced during the transition from preschool to primary school. When learning-risk status was considered, at-risk children demonstrated lower overall fluency. However, within this group, those with mature grips performing meaningful tasks showed faster growth rates, suggesting that motor maturity may partially compensate for learning vulnerability under favorable task conditions. title: Advancing teachers’ linguistic knowledge through a large-scale professional learning and development initiative
text_snippet: Advancing teachers’ linguistic knowledge through a large-scale professional learning and development initiative Abstract This study investigated the enhancement of teachers’ linguistic knowledge, skills, pedagogy, and self-rated ability within a large-scale implementation of early literacy instruction in New Zealand. Data were collected from pre- and post-learning surveys from 592 educators enrolled in online professional learning and development (PLD). Linguistic knowledge scores across phonics, phonological awareness, and morphology increased from 56–70% correct prior to PLD to 81–89% after PLD. Mixed-effects models examining predictors of change in knowledge and self-rated ability indicated that educators with lower levels of linguistic knowledge and lower self-rated ability made the most growth from pre-test to post-test. Further, self-rated ability increased more for less experienced educators. Online PLD with the practical application of linguistic knowledge and skills may be a useful strategy to enhance teachers’ linguistic knowledge at scale and within regular teaching contexts.

title: Within- and cross-language pathways from morphological awareness to reading comprehension in Chinese-English bilingual children
text_snippet: Within- and cross-language pathways from morphological awareness to reading comprehension in Chinese-English bilingual children Abstract Morphological awareness is a critical predictor of reading comprehension, yet its direct and indirect contributions within and across languages remain complex in bilingual children, particularly in typologically distinct language pairs. We examined pathways from morphological awareness to reading comprehension within and across first language (L1) Chinese and second language (L2) English in Chinese-English bilinguals. A cross-sectional sample of 467 Hong Kong students in Grade 2 ( n = 150, age = 8.10 years), Grade 5 ( n = 158, age = 11.19 years), and Grade 8 ( n = 159, age = 13.79 years) completed measures of morphological awareness, vocabulary, word reading, and reading comprehension in both L1 and L2. Grade-specific structural equation models showed that L1 morphological awareness predicted L1 reading comprehension indirectly via vocabulary in Grade 2, but directly in Grades 5 and 8. L2 morphological awareness predicted L2 reading comprehension directly and indirectly via vocabulary and word reading in Grade 2, directly in Grade 5, and directly and indirectly via vocabulary in Grade 8. title: The relationship between spelling ability, motivation and self-efficacy
text_snippet: The relationship between spelling ability, motivation and self-efficacy Abstract A wealth of research has established the importance of affective factors in understanding children’s reading and writing outcomes. However, little research has explored the role of affective factors in understanding children’s spelling ability. The present study explored the relationship between spelling ability, motivation and self-efficacy. A total of 194 children of primary school age (8–11 years old) completed measures of spelling ability, motivation and self-efficacy at one time point. The findings reported spelling ability to have a moderate positive correlation with spelling self-efficacy, intrinsic spelling motivation, and extrinsic spelling motivation. Confirmatory factor analysis supported a multidimensional structure in which the lower-order factors loaded onto three distinct higher-order intrinsic spelling motivation, extrinsic spelling motivation, and spelling self-efficacy higher-order constructs, providing evidence for the conceptual separation of these affective components. title: Examining the contribution of segmental, suprasegmental, and non-linguistic skills to early word reading in Spanish-speaking preschoolers
text_snippet: Examining the contribution of segmental, suprasegmental, and non-linguistic skills to early word reading in Spanish-speaking preschoolers Abstract Suprasegmental phonology, encompassing the rhythmic elements of spoken language, plays a significant role in early reading acquisition. Despite growing evidence of its importance, the relationships among suprasegmental and segmental phonological skills, non-linguistic rhythmic abilities and early reading development remain insufficiently specified. The present study examines how these skills contribute to early word reading in Spanish-speaking preschoolers. A total of 250 five-year-old children were assessed on segmental phonology, suprasegmental phonology (stress awareness), non-linguistic rhythmic skills, basic cognitive abilities and word reading. A predictive model of early reading was tested using structural equation modelling. The results obtained indicated that non-linguistic rhythm significantly predicted stress awareness, and that both non-linguistic rhythm and stress awareness predicted phonological awareness. In turn, phonological awareness and non-linguistic rhythm directly predicted word reading performance. title: Early literacy profiles and written language outcomes in children with and without language disorder
text_snippet: Early literacy profiles and written language outcomes in children with and without language disorder Abstract Children with Language Disorders (LD) are at elevated risk for Written Language Difficulties (WLD), including deficits in word recognition, fluency, spelling, and reading comprehension. However, this population is highly heterogeneous, and early identification of children at risk for WLD requires approaches that capture individual variability. Despite growing interest in early literacy profiling in children with LD, few studies include longitudinal data or a control group, limiting the generalizability of findings and the examination of how early profiles relate to later written language outcomes. This longitudinal study examined early literacy profiles in children with and without LD and assessed their associations with Grade 2 written language skills. Early literacy was assessed in 87 French-speaking children midway through kindergarten, before formal literacy instruction. title: Emotion transmission in the home literacy environment: a model of parents’ reading enjoyment, parental reading support, adolescents’ reading self-concept, and adolescents’ reading enjoyment
text_snippet: Emotion transmission in the home literacy environment: a model of parents’ reading enjoyment, parental reading support, adolescents’ reading self-concept, and adolescents’ reading enjoyment Abstract The current study examines the associations between parents’ reading enjoyment and adolescents’ reading enjoyment within the home literacy environment, with particular attention to the mediating roles of parental reading support and adolescents’ reading self-concept. Structural equation modeling was conducted using data from PISA 2018, based on a representative sample of 6037 15-year-old students from 152 schools in Hong Kong. The results indicated that parents’ reading enjoyment was directly associated with adolescents’ reading enjoyment, although the effect size was small. Moreover, parents’ reading enjoyment was indirectly associated with adolescents’ reading enjoyment through parental reading support and adolescents’ reading self-concept. In addition, parental reading support and adolescents’ reading self-concept formed a sequential pathway linking parents’ and adolescents’ reading enjoyment. These findings underscore the importance of family-related factors in shaping adolescents’ reading enjoyment.

title: Immersive storybook promotes vocabulary knowledge among children at risk of specific learning disorder (SLD)
text_snippet: Immersive storybook promotes vocabulary knowledge among children at risk of specific learning disorder (SLD) Abstract Language and literacy difficulties may emerge at an early age and position children as at risk of specific learning disorders (SLD) in those areas. In this spirit, the current study examined the added value of a research-based intervention in the form of an immersive storybook for supporting vocabulary knowledge, story comprehension, word spelling, and reading motivation in children at risk of SLD. While the positive effects of electronic storybooks (e-books or digital books) on literacy knowledge are empirically research based, research on the effects of immersive learning environments remains limited. Participants in this study were 69 first-grade children ( M age = 82.86, SD = 5.06) identified as children at risk of SLD in language and literacy skills, who were randomly divided into three groups: an i-book group (immersive storybook), an e-book group (tablet-based storybook), and a control group that received traditional classroom instruction. The intervention groups completed five sessions of direct vocabulary word learning of 12 target words. title: Predictors of reading comprehension in children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder: a systematic review
text_snippet: Predictors of reading comprehension in children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder: a systematic review Abstract Reading comprehension is a critical academic skill that frequently presents a significant challenge for children and adolescents with an Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) diagnosis. Meta-analytic evidence indicates that while individuals with ASD often demonstrate intact word decoding skills, they typically exhibit a lower ability in reading comprehension, particularly when engaging in inferential reasoning and contextual integration. While previous research has focused on reading comprehension in students with a diagnosis of ASD, few studies have thoroughly examined it in those without intellectual disabilities (ASD-WID) or comprehensively analyzed all relevant predictors. Hence, this systematic review examines the reading comprehension of this population compared to that of typically developing (TD) peers and the primary predictors of reading comprehension of students with a diagnosis of ASD-WID. Systematic searches in Web of Science, PubMed, ERIC, PsycArticles, and Scopus for articles published between January 2016 and September 2024 yielded 12 studies meeting the inclusion criteria. title: Relations of first-grade teacher knowledge with gains for students at risk for reading difficulties
text_snippet: Relations of first-grade teacher knowledge with gains for students at risk for reading difficulties Abstract This study used the Teacher Understanding of Literacy Constructs and Evidence-Based Instructional Practices (TULIP) survey to measure 93 Grade 1 teachers’ beginning-of-year knowledge within five domains (phonological awareness; phonics/decoding/encoding; reading fluency; oral language; reading comprehension) and reading performance in those domains at beginning and end of year for 205 students at risk for reading difficulties in teachers’ classrooms. Teacher knowledge to support phonological awareness development was positively associated with student gains on one of two related literacy measures; knowledge to teach phonics/decoding/encoding was positively associated with student gains on five of seven related literacy measures; knowledge related to oral language development was associated with student gains on one of four related literacy measures, and knowledge to teach reading comprehension was associated with student gains on two of two related literacy measures. title: Examining the small-group reading instruction of K-5 teachers who completed science of reading-aligned professional development
text_snippet: Examining the small-group reading instruction of K-5 teachers who completed science of reading-aligned professional development Abstract This study examined the K-5 reading instruction of teachers who completed LETRS professional development. Using an exploratory video analysis tool called the RIVOT, researchers examined the frequency of several instructional practices across all five components of reading along with lesson quality. Researchers also investigated potential differences of implementation across grade levels and reading ability levels. Findings indicate that although most teachers successfully utilized explicit instruction and modeling along with several research-based instructional practices across reading components, some still engaged in problematic practices (e.g., using context or images to support word reading). Practical differences were observed across grade levels and ability levels; however, no differences were statistically significant.

title: The role of radical-with-dual-coding, copying, and phonological approaches for NCS young learners in Chinese characters acquisition and memory retention
text_snippet: The role of radical-with-dual-coding, copying, and phonological approaches for NCS young learners in Chinese characters acquisition and memory retention Abstract How do non-Chinese-speaking (NCS) young learners acquire Chinese characters most effectively under brief instruction? This preliminary study compared three approaches—radical-with-dual-coding mnemonics, copying, and phonological instruction, on character acquisition and retention among NCS young learners in Hong Kong. The copying approach emphasized stroke order, directionality, and structure through motor practice. The phonological approach focused on sound-form correspondence using phonetic cues. The radical-with-dual-coding approach paired characters with simple visual pictographs and concise English prompts to support form-meaning learning. Using a counterbalanced within-subjects design, 95 participants comprising 39 preschoolers (K2-3, aged 5–6) and 56 primary students (P1-2, aged 7–8) learned 21 characters assumed to be unfamiliar, with 7 characters taught under each approach. On the immediate test, the radical-with-dual-coding approach showed the highest mean performance overall and significantly outperformed the copying approach, although its pairwise difference from the phonological approach was not significant. title: A survey study of teacher preparation programs and writing methods instruction in the United States
text_snippet: A survey study of teacher preparation programs and writing methods instruction in the United States Abstract This study seeks to understand the elements and manner of writing methods instruction (WMI) provided in elementary and special education teacher preparation program (TPP) courses at institutions of higher education across eight states. TPPs were selected based upon three criteria: (1) low, middle, or high performance on English language arts Common Core State Standards-aligned assessments; (2) geographic location across four quadrants of the United States; and (3) state literacy policies and whether teacher certification exams required elementary or special education teachers to demonstrate knowledge of science of reading (SOR) elements. A mixed methods design included analyses of TPP survey responses and syllabi provided by the program respondents. Research questions sought to understand which courses in elementary and special education programs included WMI across the selected states, how this instruction was reflected in course syllabi, and whether there were differences among programs located in states based on student outcomes and policy. title: Adolescents’ comprehension of single vs. multiple digital sources
text_snippet: Adolescents’ comprehension of single vs. multiple digital sources Abstract The capability to understand information originating from multiple documents is a central component of learning with digital media. We tested theory-based predictions that multiple source reading is cognitively more demanding than single source reading, such that comprehension accuracy is lower for multiple source reading, and that successful multiple source comprehension is more reliant on effort, i.e., the time spent on the reading task. Using PISA-2018 data from 44 countries ( N = 341,591), we tested the effect of source type (single vs. multiple), time on task, and their interaction on reading comprehension, while statistically controlling for student and item-level confounds. Our results supported the theory-based predictions that multiple source comprehension presents particular challenges to comprehension and that longer time on task is particularly beneficial to comprehension when dealing with multiple sources. Providing students with support with how best to use this additional time while processing multiple sources thus appears particularly pressing.

title: Literacy development and sleep habits across the second-grade school year
text_snippet: Literacy development and sleep habits across the second-grade school year Abstract Second grade is a key period in reading acquisition, when children consolidate decoding and strengthen orthographic, phonological, and semantic representations through sustained instruction and practice. Because sleep is linked to learning and memory consolidation in childhood, we examined whether children’s self-reported sleep habits are reflected in literacy levels and within-year literacy growth in a socioeconomically disadvantaged school context. Participants were 309 Hebrew-speaking second graders from five public schools, assessed at the beginning (T1) and end (T2) of the school year. Sleep habits were measured with the Sleep Self-Report (SSR); children were classified at T1 as poor sleepers or good sleepers using k-means clustering on three SSR subscales (bedtime behavior, sleep behavior, daytime sleepiness). Literacy performance included orthographic word identification, phonological decoding, reading comprehension, spelling, and vocabulary in pointed Hebrew. Over the year, total sleep problems, bedtime behavior, and sleep behavior improved, with greater improvement among poor sleepers, whereas daytime sleepiness showed no measurable change. title: The reading process in bilingual and monolingual children: fluency as a mediating mechanism in a morphologically complex and transparent language
text_snippet: The reading process in bilingual and monolingual children: fluency as a mediating mechanism in a morphologically complex and transparent language Abstract This study examines how native language status shapes the reading process in a morphologically rich and orthographically transparent language, focusing on reading fluency as a mediating mechanism linking bilingualism to reading comprehension. Participants were 330 primary school children in Grades 2 and 4 from low socioeconomic backgrounds, including 164 monolingual Turkish-speaking children and 166 Kurdish–Turkish bilingual children. Reading performance was assessed using grade-appropriate narrative and expository texts from the reading skills assessment tool (RSAT). Reading fluency was indexed by text reading time, total correct words, and correct words per minute, while comprehension was measured through responses to comprehension questions. Results indicated that bilingual children demonstrated lower reading fluency and comprehension than monolingual peers across text types. Fluency indicators were associated with comprehension outcomes among bilingual readers but not among monolinguals. title: From symmetry to asymmetry in sentence representation: the role of literacy and syntax in spatial bias development
text_snippet: From symmetry to asymmetry in sentence representation: the role of literacy and syntax in spatial bias development Abstract The world’s languages exhibit a wide variety of reading and writing directions: scripts may run from left to right, as in German or English; from right to left, as in Arabic or Hebrew; from top to bottom, such as in Chinese or Japanese; or even from bottom to top, as in Tagbanwa (although this script is then read in horizontal rows). The directionality of a writing system is deeply embedded in the perceptual and motor routines of its users, shaping a wide range of spatial behaviors. Mastery of a language and its script influences spatial cognition in ways that reflect the orientation of that writing system (Bergen & Chan, 2005). Beyond its impact on spatial behavior, literacy acquisition may therefore be understood as a broader process of conceptual socialization. This process shapes cognitive preferences that extend beyond reading or writing, potentially constraining or facilitating the subsequent acquisition of scripts with different directionalities. In this paper, we examine how reading and writing direction influences the visual representation of spoken sentences with different syntactic structures.

title: From stories to literacy: oral narrative macrostructure and reading comprehension in bilingual children
text_snippet: From stories to literacy: oral narrative macrostructure and reading comprehension in bilingual children Abstract Narratives have been an important tool in assessing children’s language skills. However, research on the contributions of narratives to literacy has been limited in bilinguals, especially in non-English language contexts. This longitudinal study investigated whether oral narrative macrostructure in kindergarten, assessed in both the first language (L1) and the second language (L2), uniquely predicts reading comprehension three years later. Participants were 54 Russian-German and Turkish-German bilingual children who completed oral narrative tasks ("telling") in both L1 and L2 in kindergarten. German word-level reading comprehension was assessed in Grade 1 and German text-level reading comprehension in Grade 3. Age in kindergarten, language group (Russian- vs. Turkish-German), word-level reading comprehension, and narrative length were included as control variables. title: Interrelationships among parental reading attitudes, first-graders’ reading self-beliefs, and L2 Chinese reading performance
text_snippet: Interrelationships among parental reading attitudes, first-graders’ reading self-beliefs, and L2 Chinese reading performance Abstract Under Hong Kong’s “biliterate and trilingual” language policy, immigrant students often face considerable challenges in reading Chinese. While parental involvement and children’s psychological factors are known to play critical roles in children’s reading development, there remains a lack of research focusing on the factors’ interplay and their effects on second language (L2) Chinese reading, specifically within the unique sociolinguistic context of Hong Kong. To address this gap, this study investigated the influence of parental reading attitudes on reading self-beliefs of first-grade L2 Chinese students and their reading performance. Path analysis results revealed that parental reading attitudes indirectly influenced first-grade students’ L2 Chinese reading performance through reading self-concept and self-efficacy, with self-concept mediating this effect. Self-efficacy had a stronger direct impact on reading performance, while self-concept indirectly contributed via self-efficacy. title: Home factors for critical reading skills among parents of fourth, sixth, and eighth graders
text_snippet: Home factors for critical reading skills among parents of fourth, sixth, and eighth graders Abstract Given the current flux of information of varying quality and trustworthiness, critical reading skills (e.g., evaluating, comparing, and integrating information and related sources) are needed from an early age. While there is evidence that many parents support their children’s basic reading skills by teaching decoding or by reading books with their children, it is less clear how critical reading skills are supported at home during later school years. To address this gap, this study examined the prevalence, variability, and factor structure of a parental questionnaire on the home factors for critical reading using data from Finland. In addition, we investigated the roles of the child’s and parent’s genders, parents’ education levels, and the amount of reading materials at home in explaining the home factors for critical reading. To this end, parents of fourth graders ( n G 4 = 149), sixth graders ( n G 6 = 213), and eighth graders ( n G 8 = 226) responded to a questionnaire. title: The effect of motor sequence on written word production of a new script moderated by script experience and visual complexity
text_snippet: The effect of motor sequence on written word production of a new script moderated by script experience and visual complexity Abstract Despite the rise of digital technologies, handwriting remains more effective than typing for learning visual forms and writing words. The visual analysis hypothesis suggests that displayed continuous movement trajectories benefit handwriting by encouraging detailed visual analysis of a script. Using Korean Hangul characters as novel visual forms, this study focused on the visuomotor component of written form reproduction, and examined the effectiveness of motor-sequence presentation for written-form reproduction, as well as whether this effectiveness was modulated by native-script experience and visual complexity. Seventy-eight college-level participants (40 native readers of a nonlinear script, Chinese, and 38 readers of linear scripts such as Spanish) completed a delayed copying task. Hangul characters varied in visual complexity (low, medium, high) and were presented either with or without animated motor sequences. title: Cognitive-linguistic predictors of L1 Chinese and L2 Malay word reading in Malaysian Chinese children
text_snippet: Cognitive-linguistic predictors of L1 Chinese and L2 Malay word reading in Malaysian Chinese children Abstract The present study examined the cognitive-linguistic correlates of L1 Chinese and L2 Malay word reading accuracy and fluency among Grade 2 Malaysian Chinese children. Seventy-five children were tested on phonological awareness, delayed copying, morphological awareness, and rapid automatized naming (RAN), along with word reading skills across both Chinese and Malay languages. Results of hierarchical regression analyses revealed that Chinese morphological awareness and RAN predicted both Chinese reading accuracy and fluency after controlling for age and non-verbal IQ. Only Malay delayed copying predicted Malay reading accuracy, while Malay delayed copying, morphological awareness, and RAN predicted Malay reading fluency. In addition, Malay delayed copying predicted both Malay reading accuracy and fluency even after controlling for the effects of Malay phonological and morphological processing. These findings support the importance of understanding L1 Chinese literacy in Malaysia, a non-dominant Chinese society, to help uncover the universality of Chinese literacy acquisition. text_snippet: Eye movements in natural silent reading and their motor and cognitive correlates: a large-scale population-based study of pre-adolescents Abstract Eye tracking research has been instrumental in deepening our understanding of the reading process. Growing evidence links individual differences in eye movement patterns to cognitive abilities, but these associations remain underexplored in developing readers. This study examined the feasibility of implementing large-scale eye tracking in a population-based sample of developing readers, and examined the associations between eye movement patterns, reading skill, and cognitive and motor components. Eye movement data were obtained from 713 Dutch pre-adolescents (mean age: 9.8 years), with other assessments including word reading, motor control, phonological short-term memory, non-verbal intelligence, and vocabulary knowledge. Carefully addressing demographic effects, results from linear regression analyses revealed subtle but distinct associations between individual differences in cognitive and motor skills and temporal and spatial eye movement measures.
